clue.text: Take flight, carrying Charlie, following sea transportation issue

indicators.note: What you carry you hold inside you.
To follow is to come along behind.

blocks.note: a sub is a submarine, the usual short form
to jet off somewhere is to take a flight
Charlie is C in the NATO alphabet

explanation.walkthrough: 'Take flight' wants to be fleeing and 'issue' wants to be a magazine or a problem. Neither reading survives, and the letter goes inside the verb rather than after it.
explanation.definitionFit: 'Issue' in the sense of the matter under discussion: the issue before a meeting is the topic on the table, not a problem or a magazine.

clue.text: Principally, social categorisation has one overwhelming limitation – it’s divided by class

indicators.note: The principal part of a word is where it starts, so this asks for the opening letter of each word that follows.

blocks.clueFragment: social categorisation has one overwhelming limitation
blocks.note: six words standing in a row, each giving up the letter it begins with

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is sociology, where class means social rank; the definition means the classroom sort. A principal runs one of these, which is the setter winking at his own indicator.
explanation.definitionFit: Pupils are split into classes, so the phrase describes the institution by how it organises its day rather than by naming it outright.

clue.text: Chief briefly interrupted by a doctor turning tables

indicators.note: Said briefly, a word is cut short, and here that means losing the last of its four letters.
An interruption arrives in the middle of what is being said, so the new letters land inside the word rather than after it.
Something turning ends up facing the other way, so the abbreviation is written from its last letter to its first.

blocks.note: the chief of a firm is the boss, docked here to three letters
the article is taken at face value, as a single letter
a doctor is DR in the standard abbreviation, and it arrives the other way round

explanation.walkthrough: 'Turning tables' reads as one phrase and does two separate jobs: the doctor is what turns, and the tables are the definition sitting quietly at the end.
explanation.definitionFit: A board is a plank and so the table made from one — 'board and lodging' still means the meals taken at somebody's table.

clue.text: French milk served up in German city’s just what we need

definitions.note: The answer is plural while the definition carries no -s; a phrase like 'what we need' stands for a whole set of things at once, so it substitutes fairly.

indicators.note: Serving something up presents it the other way about, and 'up' is the direction a down entry reverses in.
'in' is the plainest containment instruction there is.

blocks.note: Essen is a city in the Ruhr, a setter's favourite for its vowels
milk in French is lait, and this entry runs down the grid, so it is set out from the bottom
the possessive tacks its own letter onto the city

explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophe-s does two jobs at once: it is the final letter of the assembly and the 'is' joining wordplay to definition. Setters allow themselves that double duty.
explanation.definitionFit: Essentials are the things you cannot do without, so 'just what we need' names them by the test they have to pass.

clue.text: Instructor’s express disapproval with soldiers

blocks.note: the noise you make to show you disapprove is written tut
OR is 'other ranks', the British Army's term for soldiers who are not officers

explanation.walkthrough: Two of the plainest conventions there are, laid end to end. The soldiers one is worth owning: OR turns up whenever a clue mentions men or ranks.
explanation.definitionFit: A tutor instructs one pupil or a small group — the private or university teacher, rather than anyone standing in front of a class.

clue.text: Recognises love shared by you and me?

blocks.note: hon is the affectionate address, short for honey
what belongs to the two of us together is ours

explanation.walkthrough: 'Love' is the term of endearment, not the tennis nought a solver reaches for first, and the question mark is the setter admitting the short form.
explanation.definitionFit: To honour somebody is to recognise them formally — the verb behind an honours list, where public recognition is the whole point.

clue.text: Smell I left before I ate is cause to feel bad

indicators.note: 'before' fixes the order of the pieces: what is named first is written first, and the eating comes last.

blocks.note: in British usage something that hums smells, and not pleasantly
the setter's I taken at face value, then L, the standard abbreviation for left
the I comes round a second time and 'ate' contributes its own three letters

explanation.walkthrough: Five short pieces in a row, and the same letter I is clued twice — setters count each appearance separately, so spotting one does not mean you have both.
explanation.definitionFit: To humiliate is to make somebody feel small in front of others: 'cause to feel bad' with the particular sting of wounded pride.

clue.text: N American, African, Asian, Oceanian or even from the Antarctic!

definitions.text: N American, African, Asian, Oceanian or even from the Antarctic!

blocks.note: read as nationalities this is a list of people, which is the reading the surface is pushing
the continent with no nation of its own still has collectors' paper money, and the exclamation mark is the setter enjoying that

explanation.walkthrough: There is no separable wordplay here — the whole sentence is the definition. Read the adjectives as currencies rather than as peoples and the answer is paper money.
explanation.definitionFit: The clue lists where paper money is issued, and the last item is the joke: the one continent without a country of its own.

clue.text: Open-minded nude American Bishop is sacked

indicators.note: A sacked city has been ransacked and left in disarray, and letters in disarray are letters to be put in a new order.

blocks.note: the word is here for its four letters
A is the standard abbreviation for American
B is the bishop in chess notation
the little verb is fodder too, contributing two more letters

explanation.walkthrough: The word 'is' looks like joinery and is really material. Setters count every letter offered, and a two-letter word is the easiest one to leave out of the count.
explanation.definitionFit: Somebody unbiased leans neither way, which is what open-minded describes: willing to weigh a case without arriving with the verdict.

clue.text: Watch Spooner’s electronics series?

indicators.note: The Reverend Spooner traded the opening sounds of two words, so naming him is the instruction to swap them over.

blocks.note: electronics is tech, and it gives its opening sound away in exchange for an SP
a spate of things is a run of them one after another, and it collects the T that tech gave up

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark admits the looseness: tech for electronics and a spate for a series are both everyday shorthand rather than dictionary equivalents.
explanation.definitionFit: To spectate is to watch from the side rather than take part — the verb built backwards out of 'spectator'.

clue.text: Oversees advancement of ecstasy in hell

indicators.note: Ecstasy is E by the usual drug convention, and advancing it moves that letter one place forward through the others.

blocks.note: hell in Greek myth is Hades, the underworld itself

explanation.walkthrough: Nothing is scrambled at random here. One letter steps forward and everything else keeps its place, which is why the indicator names the letter it is moving.
explanation.definitionFit: To head a department is to be in charge of it, so the -s form answers 'oversees' as a verb rather than naming any body part.

clue.text: Schedule board to pursue Master embroiled in relationship

indicators.note: To pursue is to chase along behind, so the furniture word is written after everything the clue has already built.
Someone embroiled in an affair is caught up inside it, so the abbreviation sits within the bond rather than beside it.

blocks.note: a tie is a bond between two people
M is the standard abbreviation for Master
board and table are the same piece of furniture, as in 'board and lodging'

explanation.walkthrough: The surface hints at gossip about a schoolmaster; the M is only an abbreviation. Note that 2 down makes the same board-for-table swap in the opposite direction.
explanation.definitionFit: A schedule set out by the clock is a timetable — the British word for the printed plan of a school day or a train service.

clue.text: Normally, on the other hand, start off cautiously after loud noise

indicators.note: To start something off is to begin it, and beginning this adverb means taking its opening letter away.
'after' says where the trimmed adverb goes.

blocks.note: the word that offers the alternative is or
a din is a continuous loud noise
the adverb wanted is warily, and its first letter has been started off

explanation.walkthrough: 'Start off cautiously' reads as advice about how to begin something, which is the trap: it is an instruction to take the first letter off an adverb.
explanation.definitionFit: Ordinarily means in the ordinary run of things, so it does the job 'normally' does — a statement of habit rather than of what is normal.

clue.text: Reality show tailing female

indicators.note: To tail somebody is to follow along behind them, so the performance is written after the letter it trails.

blocks.note: F is the standard abbreviation for female
an act is a turn shown on stage

explanation.walkthrough: 'Reality show' is the trap — it reads as the television genre. The definition stops after the first word, and the show belongs to the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: A fact is what is genuinely the case, and 'reality' names the same thing as a noun: the truth of things, not a TV format.

clue.text: Nice places being arranged – somewhere to accommodate writers

indicators.note: Things being arranged are being put into a new order, which is exactly what happens to these ten letters.

blocks.note: the two words are here for their ten letters

explanation.walkthrough: 'Nice places' wants to be the French Riviera, and the capital letter is fair because the phrase opens the clue. The writers are implements, not people.
explanation.definitionFit: The thing accommodates pens and pencils, and 'writers' is the setter's word for the implements that do the writing.

clue.text: Being out of order, criticise and put down setter, heartless nut!

indicators.note: The heart of a three-letter word is its middle letter, and a heartless word has had that letter taken out.

blocks.note: to dis someone is to criticise them, in the slang spelling
to put something down is to place it
the setter is the person writing the clue, so 'setter' is ME
the U at its centre is the heart that goes

explanation.walkthrough: 'Out of order' means out of its proper place here, not broken or badly behaved. The setter-is-ME convention is worth owning: it turns up in every grid.
explanation.definitionFit: Displacement is the state of having been shifted out of position, which is what 'out of order' means when order is arrangement rather than repair.

clue.text: 1Ds for young, strait-laced group of stars

blocks.note: prim means stiffly proper and easily shocked
Aries the ram is a constellation, the first sign of the zodiac

explanation.walkthrough: The definition points at another clue: read '1Ds' as the answer to 1 down, in the plural. Cross-references like this are always to the solved word, never to the clue.
explanation.definitionFit: 1 down's answer is SCHOOL, and in Britain primaries are the schools that take children up to about eleven.

clue.text: Gin diet’s crazy – and most dull!

indicators.note: What is crazy has gone out of its right order, which is the instruction to put these letters into a different one.

blocks.note: the letters of both words, apostrophe and all, are the material

explanation.walkthrough: The dash marks the join: 'crazy' finishes the wordplay and 'most dull' begins the definition. Guardian setters use it where a link word would otherwise go.
explanation.definitionFit: Dingy means grimy and gloomy, so the dingiest room is the drabbest — dull in the sense of dim and colourless, not boring.

clue.text: Mood elevation when drinking Tango, putting away litres!

indicators.note: To drink something is to take it inside you, so the letter goes within the word that swallows it.
Putting something away is stowing it out of sight, so the letter it names leaves the word altogether.

blocks.note: elevation is height above sea level
Tango is T in the NATO alphabet
l is the symbol for litre, and this is the letter taken off

explanation.walkthrough: Tango is a British fizzy orange drink as well as the NATO alphabet's T, which is what lets the surface read as a night out rather than a spelling lesson.
explanation.definitionFit: An attitude is the stance somebody takes towards things, so 'mood' fits as the settled frame of mind rather than a passing feeling.

clue.text: Another order for gilt Nile scene excluding special information

indicators.note: Order here means arrangement rather than command, and another arrangement of the same letters is what the clue wants.
What is excluded is kept out, so the letter named next never joins the letters being shuffled.

blocks.note: the three words are here for their thirteen letters, not their picture
S is the standard abbreviation for special, and it is the letter left out

explanation.walkthrough: The deletion happens before the shuffle, so count the fodder first: thirteen letters offered, one taken away, twelve to be rearranged into the enumeration.
explanation.definitionFit: Information gathered about an enemy or a rival is intelligence — the spy's sense of the word, which is why the surface talks about scenes and exclusions.

clue.text: It may be carrying files from the French supporting Eastern currency

indicators.note: A support sits underneath what it holds up, and underneath in a down entry means later, so this piece goes at the bottom.

blocks.note: the dong is the currency of Vietnam
'le' is one of the French words for 'the'

explanation.walkthrough: Foreign-word clues like this one lean on schoolroom French, and the direction word is doing real work: in a down entry, 'supporting' means below and so later.
explanation.definitionFit: A dongle is the small stick that plugs into a computer to carry files or unlock software, so the whole phrase describes one by what it does.

clue.text: State agreement for rise

indicators.note: To state something is to say it out loud, so what gets written down is whatever the spoken word sounds like.

blocks.note: agreement given is assent, spelt with a double S and sounding identical to the climb

explanation.walkthrough: Two spellings, one sound. Only the crossing letters tell you which one the grid wants, which is why homophone clues are worth leaving until a few crossers are in.
explanation.definitionFit: An ascent is a climb upwards and 'rise' names that same movement as a noun: the going up, rather than the thing that goes up.

clue.text: Giganet’s first free network

indicators.note: 'first' asks only for the opening letter of the invented company standing in front of it.

blocks.note: the opening letter of that made-up company's name
to be rid of something is to be free of it

explanation.walkthrough: Giganet is invented for the surface and only its initial matters. The definition is electrical, which is what makes the technology surface sound plausible.
explanation.definitionFit: The grid is the network of cables distributing electricity around a country — Britain calls its own the National Grid.

clue.text: Flying creature with claws circling international groups of soldiers

indicators.note: Something circling goes right round the thing it circles.

blocks.note: the flying creature wanted is the only mammal that does it properly
the claws of a bird of prey are its talons
I is the standard abbreviation for international

explanation.walkthrough: The surface shows one bird — flying, clawed and circling — while the parse needs three separate pieces out of it, and the circling belongs to the letters, not the bird.
explanation.definitionFit: A battalion is an army unit of several hundred troops, so the plural names groups of soldiers by their formal size.

clue.text: Disorganised teens stressed

indicators.note: What is disorganised has lost the arrangement it came in, so the word beside it is to be put into another.

blocks.note: the five letters offered are the whole of the material

explanation.walkthrough: Three words, and the only work is deciding which two belong together. 'Disorganised teens' is the wordplay; the last word alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Somebody tense is strung tight and on edge, which is what 'stressed' describes — the adjective for the person, not the verb for emphasis.

clue.text: Antifa illegally concealing collapse

indicators.note: To conceal something is to hide it inside something else, so the letters are already there in order, not waiting to be shuffled.

blocks.note: the letters run consecutively across the join between the two words

explanation.walkthrough: Hidden words hide because the surface is doing all the shouting: two political words in a row, with the answer lying flat across the gap between them.
explanation.definitionFit: Collapse here means coming to nothing — a scheme that collapses has not fallen over, it has simply not worked.

clue.text: Teaching can die out if it’s disordered

blocks.note: three ordinary words in a row, offered for their letters

explanation.walkthrough: The fodder hides by being a sentence with an opinion in it. Reading 'can die out' as a gloomy prediction is exactly what stops you counting its letters.
explanation.definitionFit: 'Teaching' as a noun names the activity, and education is that activity taken as a whole — schooling rather than a single lesson.

clue.text: Swing headless fish

indicators.note: The head of a word is the letter it begins with, so a headless word has lost its first letter.

blocks.note: something swinging loosely from a hook dangles
the head of that swinging word is its D, and that is what goes

explanation.walkthrough: Three words and none of them does the job you expect. 'Fish' is the definition, in the sense of what an angler does, and 'Swing' is the word to behead.
explanation.definitionFit: To angle is to fish with rod and line — the verb behind 'angler', and the sense that keeps the word alive outside geometry.

clue.text: Wood surrounding the outskirts of Blackpool gets three times bigger

indicators.note: What surrounds something wraps all the way round it, so the woodland word opens up and closes again on both sides.
The outskirts of a town are its outer edges, so the edges of the word are the two letters wanted.

blocks.note: a wood is a stand of trees
the outer letters of the resort's name, its first and its last

explanation.walkthrough: Blackpool is an English seaside resort with a tower and a pier, but the clue wants only the letters at its two ends — everything in the middle is scenery.
explanation.definitionFit: To treble is to multiply by three, so a sum that trebles has grown to three times what it was before.

clue.text: Part company in English hamlet, half-cut

indicators.note: 'in' is the plainest way of saying something goes inside.
Cut in half, the village word keeps only one of its halves, and it is the back one that survives.

blocks.note: E is the usual abbreviation for English
a hamlet is a village too small for a church, and only its back half is used
a company is a body of men, in the army sense of the word

explanation.walkthrough: 'Part company' is the phrase the surface wants and the parse cuts in two: 'Part' is the definition, 'company' the wordplay. Half-cut is British slang for tipsy.
explanation.definitionFit: An element is one part of a whole: the elements of a plan are its components, which is the sense the definition uses.
